Question: Where can I find nice Chinese food in Stockholm?
Answer: Chinese food is my middle name. Also in Stockholm. This is mostly due to Mrs Ebbert’s strict guidelines for what’s acceptable restaurant food when we go out together, but I have learned a lot from her. Having grown up in Beijing, she applies some pretty strict standards to Chinese food. Both she and I particularly like these three places in Stockholm for food: FORMOSA, in the Old Town district; in operation since 1968, it’s a Stockholm classic that serves authentic, Chinese food of the highest standard. It’s our go-to choice: PONG, a buffet restaurant chain with quite a few locations, typically in malls. Our favourite is the one in the Westfield Mall of Scandinavia, but they are generally quite fabulous - Pan Asian rather than strictly Chinese, but those Chinese things they do offer pass muster all the way, as do the other things they serve: R-ASIA Restaurant in Solna Centrum, another buffet restaurant. Pan Asian also, and they do some great barbecuing, too.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Is it normal behaviour for Swedish supermarket check out staffs not to say thank you (like part of their routines at checkout?)?
Answer: When you go through a Swedish checkout, the cashier will simply scan your wares, then wait for you to swipe your card and move on. They won’t give you the full hospitality treatment like in North America that may include polite inquiries into your health, a company slogan, and a wave goodbye with flowery proclamations of looking forward to soon being reunited at this counter with more purchases. Instead, you may get a friendly nod. If you say “hej då” as a farewell, they will be happy, and you can see it on their faces, but it may not be reciprocated. Swedish interactions presume inner harmony of all concerned as a default setting, so there is no necessity for vocalized assertions of benevolence every step of the way.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: How do Swedes act around each other?
Answer: Swedes around each other act casual, yet respectful. Always at eye height. Probably the most similar behaviour to that of the Swedes among strangers elsewhere, I have observed in Canada, France, and Argentina. You get the sense that there is a whole population that is perfectly aware of one proper way to behave, and they will do it, while also retaining full individuality in appearance and choices. As in, you are entirely yourself, and expect the same of the other, but you are using the same frequency. For an outsider observing them, there may be a bewildering sense of familiarity among strangers - almost as if everybody already knows everybody else, and just engages in any interaction calmly, comfortably, warmly - as one would when feeling strong kinship with the other. There are no real thresholds or hurdles to be overcome. Not too different also from Israel, Australia, or New Zealand. Only that the Swedes come across more refined, more genteel, and there is a barrier when it comes to speaking to strangers who are not there in a capacity of service provider or leisure seeker. In that latter case, be prepared to be ignored. Swedes have a privacy bubble they can turn on or off, like the force field of Starship Enterprise - and you will know quickly when it's on. You didn't do anything wrong if it happens to you. It's just that a Swede may decide to be invisible to strangers on any given day, and then, it's best to grant them that. Imagine you find yourself in the staff room of a university or high school. That's what Swedes act like.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Do Europeans like muscle cars?
Answer: You’ll probably find that all Europeans will appreciate a sleek body and big engine. But that’s where it splits into two camps. Camp one is probably a minority, and I count myself toward it: Guys (and gals) who are a little more mellow than the norm, have romantic feelings for North American scenery and cars, love the slow rumbling sound of a V8 engine, and find it perfectly acceptable that a sports car has a rigid rear axle and an automatic transmission, and sells at the price, and possibly to the same customer group, as a family hatchback. There aren’t many of us here. Maybe 10% of the population. The rest prefer their cars European style, meaning more refined, more expensive, and with a lot less soul, if any. I grant Alfa Romeo, Maserati, Lancia, and Jaguar special status in that assessment though.

Question: What is your favorite song and why?
Answer: I have a lot of favourite songs, but one I keep coming back to is La Gente, by the band Indios, from Argentina. It’s so easy, so airy, so natural. Just a bit of guitar, and a bit of song. It immediately puts me somewhere by a wild river in the Andes, somewhere between Mendoza and Bariloche. Light, honest, dreamy, fun music at the serene end of the world. The other one is Os alquimistas estão Chegando, by Jorge Ben Jor, from Brazil. Or Tal Vez me Eviquivoque, again by Indios. Or Escarcha, or Sin Ti, by Roberto Rojas. Oh well, and then, there’s Recuerdos de Ypacarai, by Luis Alberto del Parana. Or Amor, Amor, also by him. Corny as hell, but that’s why we do it. Or Nú Com A Minha Música by Marisa Monte. And O Que Me Importa, also by her. I think I could just sit in a bar in Buenos Aires or Rio de Janeiro and listen to music for the rest of my life. Romantically, I’m forever stuck in the 1960s, in South America. I so wish I could be there.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Why don't people in Europe buy air conditioners?
Answer: There is a deadly fear of power bills in Europe. I’m not kidding. My own example included. When I lived in Germany, my average monthly power bill was about 50 Euros, and it raised the same hackles as income tax raises with Americans. It seemed an existential threat to my existence. Not because it was that much money, but because it just seemed so… imposed. There is nothing you can do about your power bill, and there is nothing you can do about your income tax. Maybe the power bill is 50 Euros this month, but it could be 500, or 5000, if the mysterious powers that be so decide. Of course it won’t be, but the feeling is there. I paid 500 dollars a month in New Zealand and 200 Euros in France and 3000 kronor in Sweden and never blinked, but somehow, most of Europe just hasn’t got the nerve to man up to a power bill. And that’s how it is - an air conditioner eats power, and costs money. And the impossibility to calculate and monitor that cost as it occurs is too much for most Europeans. They believe they will be bankrupt after one month of using an air conditioner. I suggest installing power meters that display Euros, and eventually, Europeans will understand and learn to trust air cons. To illustrate the psychology behind it, I know a German lady here in my village in Sweden who heats with fire wood because it saves her 80 Euros a month over electricity. Well, that’s just crazy. She could very easily afford a much higher bill than that, but she is of the opinion that “the power bill MUST NOT BE OVER 100 EUROS, ever.” To the death. It’s a psychosis.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: How are people coping with the heat in Europe?
Answer: Some of us are dealing with the heat by sheer luck. For some reason, we’ve been seeing low temperatures and rain for six weeks here now in Östersund, Mid Sweden, while my family in Germany and Austria is boiling at temperatures between 38 and 41 Celsius. I am immensely grateful for being up here. In fact, I am currently sitting in my basement TV room with my cats, running a heater. Studies actually predict that my part of Sweden is going to be more and more like that. Given the brutal heat further south, I am really glad to be here. As for my family, it seems that my parents are often retreating to the basement of their 1970s row house in Germany, or taking a dip in a lake in Austria. As temperatures sink lower in the evening, they sit outside in the breeze with a glass of white wine.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: I’m usually a very introverted person but I want to change and become an extrovert. What are some tips?
Answer: I consider myself an introvert who acts extrovert. It did not take a lot to get there. Basically, just start thinking aloud, blurt out the thoughts you’d otherwise mull over quietly in your mind first, and most importantly, start enjoying and feeding on the reactions you get from people. The latter is probably what really kept me going. I realized quickly that it is very satisfying to make people laugh, so I turned from this silent little nerd to a stand up comedian, over night. I might have been seven or eight years old, and it was a chance discovery. My mum was putting my jeans into the washing machine, and had extracted a little toy pistol I had kept in it and put it on the machine. I happened to be passing by and asked politely whether I could have the gun, or if she still needed it. It was an innocent, politeness inspired thing to say, but hilariously off. That moment changed my life. I realized I could make people laugh by saying certain things. I made it my mission to do this as often as possible, and became a far more extrovert person.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Why is kebab so popular in Europe?
Answer: There must be a version of the concept “meat wrapped in bread” in just about any culture. Hamburgers in the US, sandwiches and pies in Britain and its Commonwealth, Wurschtsemmel in Germany and Austria, smörgåsar in Sweden and the rest of the Nordics, chivitos on the Rio de la Plata delta, etc. But kebabs do one thing the others don’t take to the same length: Complexity. The kebabs you can buy in your average kebab shop in Germany or Sweden can be loaded up in ways perhaps only the American chain Subway has ever tried to rival. If I want my kebab with fifty different things, I can have my kebab with fifty different things. Sauces, salads, pickles, you name it, it’s astonishing. In Germany, they will ask you (enter Turkish accent) “mit alles?”, which is grammatically wrong, but the correct way to order a kebab, and I do respond with “mit alles”. That gives me a bread type that is superior in appeal to the spongy things the westerners come to the table with, a grilled rotisserie meat of a higher perceived quality than the minced space cows that make up American or German processed wonders, lovely sauces with a touch of the Mediterranean that presumably contain far less rocket fuel than the production optimized things you get in little plastic boxes in your bag, and finely chopped, raw veggies that bulk up the whole thing to the point where you could be forgiven for thinking you’re eating something healthy. Have you tried eating till you are full on western fast food? I know people who’ve been trying for decades and are still not done, but have taken on frightening dimensions in the process. A kebab will actually make you feel full eventually. In short, kebabs outclass their contenders in quality, healthiness, and ability to actually fill you up. (My local kebab bar from the inside).

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: How come southern countries are more relaxed than northern countries?
Answer: Ah, there it was again, the old stereotype. “Relaxed”. What is that? A society were bribes can take care of things? A place where not being punctual is the norm? A place where spending lots of time with food and family is an alternative to a career? There, it’s a useless stereotype. Built on the precept that relaxedness is laxness. And quite possibly on having been a tourist in southern places. Work in these places, and the perception will change. When you look at the World Happiness Index, you find where the truly relaxed places are. Places where things run well enough so as not to stress you out. True relaxedness requires things to be in good working order, and well-run countries provide that. Some of them may qualify as “southern”, but you’ll find more relaxedness in places northern.

In theory, I could say, show me any object, and I can do a better one, and you’ll have my response within the day; as a 3D model if you wish. I am an industrial designer, and now work for the Swedish government as an innovation advisor. Some of my ideas have over the years become reality, because other people also thought of them, and I am rarely surprised by things that pop up on the market, because usually, I will have thought of that solution before. I used to think it could make me rich and famous, but the fact is that the world actually hates new ideas and will only ever resort to them when there is no other way, or when massive marketing efforts have been undertaken to make it palatable. Industry does not want my stuff, either, because they usually have their own plans. It would be my dream to meet someone who says “Chris, what inventions have you got? Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Are the Nordic countries much different from continental Europe?
Answer: Yes, I consider the Nordics quite different from continental Europe. Perhaps a little less so in terms of mentality and culture, but definitely in terms of environment. When you are in the Nordics, you may feel that the people are very much like the Dutch, or the French. But the environment is very different from continental Europe. It’s vast, wild, and brilliantly colourful. Where I live now reminds me mostly of Alaska, Patagonia, or Canada in general. Wide open expanses of deep blue, glittering water, deep old forests, and you can drive for hours without encountering a soul. You may at times think you have time traveled, because there’s just nothing up here to tell you what year it is. You wouldn’t get that, on the continent. I just took these before lunch today. Try that in Germany or Belgium.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: What's the best way to get rid of a person in your life?
Answer: Everyone is on a journey. A road, if you will. No two roads are ever the same, unless we bend them to be. If you want to shed someone, all you need to do is do your thing, without taking into account what that might mean for the other person. And eventually, they will fall away. This can be both a strategy, and a warning.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Is it worth moving to Sweden for work?
Answer: No. If you are only doing it for materialistic reasons, don’t come. If work is the only thing on your mind, you can earn more elsewhere in a shorter time, potentially in a warmer climate, with lower taxes, all in English, in a place where everything is cheap. Sweden is worth moving to if you are in love with a mellow lifestyle with great life/ work balance, harmonious relations in life and at work, European values, a very liberal, western mindset, and a seasonal life where your environment will change fundamentally every three months, letting you experience intense periods of snowy winters, brightly coloured autumns, and warm summers with long stretches of holidays where no one works. Sweden is a cultural choice. I would hate to see anyone coming here solely for work reasons, as it would be such a waste of all the wonderfully romantic, historical, cultural, and lifestyle related aspects life in Sweden brings. This is a country where work takes a backseat, and where being human is first. Come here to enjoy life, contribute to society, experience depth. And prepare to be humble, share, and make do with a reasonable modicum.

Question: Which European country is the best liked by other Europeans?
Answer: As a European who has managed to speak to many other Europeans, I would say Italy is the most well-liked country among Europeans. Pretty much everyone has nice things to say about Italy. Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: What are some examples of one moment that has changed your fate and life?
Answer: All through my years as an undergraduate student in Canada, I dearly wished to learn the Italian language. I felt an immense affinity with Italy and its culture and music and design and landscapes, which, to be fair, I had already grown up with as a little boy in Europe. I just wanted to also speak their language, clearly with the possible intention to one day make it my home - there, or the Swiss Ticino, which I’ve always loved. Alas, it wasn’t to be. Every year, when I assembled my courses and subjects, that Italian course was either fully booked, or not happening. But I had chosen a pathway to my degree course that required me taking a foreign language, so when my final year rolled around, the friendly people at the registrar’s office put the gun to my head and said “well, Chris, time to choose a language - we have Polish, Ukrainian, Lithuanian, or Swedish; which is it gonna be?” I chose Swedish as I figured it was the one most relevant for a designer, after Italian. But I knew nothing about Sweden, and began my course with a shrug. Only days into it, I found myself ravaged by fascination about Sweden, and charmed by its language to no end. That wasn’t supposed to happen. I was supposed to turn into some guy working for Pininfarina, sipping espressos. Instead, I found myself dream-drifting into heavy snow territory with endless forests and little red houses. Almost three decades on, it’s where I live now. Didn’t see that coming.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Have you ever had an elephant in the room moment?
Answer: It only dawned on me very recently that the driving force in my life has to do with an attraction to countries that invite strangers to make them their home, and to reconcile that with the values that built me as a child. Because I want to find my home in this world. In a way, this has always been a standoff between the Americas, especially Latin America, and the Nordics. The unifying force between these two, for me, has always been their natural ease with a life vision that is modest in a naturally abundant environment, yet genuine in the human connections that life brings on. I think life is full of these strange, seeming contradictions. My life could be as fulfilled as it is here in Sweden also in Chile, Argentina, Mexico, or Paraguay. I see these as very real alternatives to where I am.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: What car model would you buy?
Answer: When it comes to buying cars, I have been following a formula for about twenty years that I’ve come up with myself. It always leads me to the best possible car: Once you realize that there is not much left over after “most reliable” that isn’t from Japan, things become quite easy. In fact, this formula has saved me from having to wade into the maze of possible offerings time and again, because if you are looking for “most reliable”, and choose from the top ten of that, you have a very manageable number of vehicles to check out. For me, the formula has been leading to Toyotas directly for the past twenty years. My current Toyota is a result of me using that formula, too. If I were to replace it these days, my choice might be a current Toyota Yaris or Corolla plug-in hybrid if I keep driving as little as I do. These are both models I can recommend without reservations to anyone, as there are very few good reasons not to have one of these. But I am also looking at the new, electric Toyota BZ4X. If the price of fuel does not come back down to about EUR 1.50 per liter where I live (it’s currently at EUR 2.40), I will be waving good bye to gasoline cars for good in about three to five years time.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Why would someone move from Germany to Sweden?
Answer: I am a German who has made the move to Sweden because I prefer living here. Sweden’s much more gentle mentality and unhurried ways appeal to me, as do its wide open landscapes and the wilderness. It’s a mellow, scenic place where everything my German value set wants to see actually exists in equal or better form than in Germany, while sparing me the bits I do not like about Germany. I suppose it’s a bit like an American moving to Canada. Up here, I can live in ways that would not be so easy in Germany - house by a lake, a few vintage cars, in a very seasonal climate that gives me dramatic, natural experiences. Germany’s climate has become one of boring, rainy winters and steamy, boiling summers. It’s no longer the lovely four season climate I grew up with. Up here though, I get my satisfying snow winters, incredible autumns, and perfectly civilized summers where sitting under the birch tree in the hammock is lovely all day long, entirely without risking sun stroke or heat exhaustion. For me, moving to Sweden has been a bit like time travel, back to the climate of my childhood in Bavaria and Austria. Mixed with a generous dose of Canadian style wilderness, friendliness, and mellowness. I think someone who really likes living in a society of northern European values, with strong, seasonal character, but wants to do so without the stress and the fast pace of Germany will find Sweden very viable. A few images from my life in Jämtland and Västernorrland: Not the predominant impressions of a life spent in Germany. Which is also not terrible, but if you can get 1st class, why settle for second? Question: How accurate is it to say that English is an immigrant language in Sweden?
Answer: English in Sweden is more the international language of business and global default communication. That’s how it is “marketed” to school children, as well. English-speaking immigrants here are not the norm. Granted, many who come here on industry- or university contracts will be using it, often for years until they become fluent in Swedish. And you’ll find English available as an option on most government websites. But the most commonly heard foreign languages here today in the street are Arabic and Somali. And yes, they are also often available website options. It comes and goes with the groups of new arrivals. At one stage, the language alternatives may well have been Italian, Greek, or Spanish here, then Turkish for a while… even Yiddish is still one of Sweden’s officially available language options. I guess once the option has been created, it sticks around.

Question: Where is the best place to go swimming in Sweden?
Answer: You have a good number of choices when it comes to going swimming in Sweden. There’s water everywhere here, and most of it is super clean - even drinking water quality. I’ve swum in Stockholm’s harbour, as some guys were fishing. I don’t think you’d see that in a lot of other capitals with big sea ports. Personally, I like swimming in lakes best, but let’s look at the full range: Salt water/ Baltic coast/ sandy beaches: The Baltic coast tends to be very mild mannered, with minimal tides, and fairly shallow waters that get quite warm in summer. The most famous ones are around Kalmar and Öland, but this photo was taken quite far north, on Alnön near Sundsvall. It’s my favourite sandy beach where I live and work. Very few Russian submarines in it, too. Salt water/ Baltic coast/ rocky beaches: This photo was taken along a stretch of coast called Höga Kusten, the High Coast. It’s between Sundsvall and Umeå, and a great place in general. In my opinion, an up and coming place that may well become the Bohuslän of the future. Salt water/ North Sea coast/ pebble beaches: This is a fairly typical scenario along the whole west coast. I like it because those rocks really charge up with sunlight during the summer, and keep the water temperature pretty even. Bohuslän especially is very famous for it. Think of it as the “Swedish Cornwall”. Salt water/ North Sea coast/ sandy beaches: You get that kind of beach along the lower part of the west coast, starting around Malmö and continuing via Lund and Helsingborg and a bit beyond. Fresh water/ lake/ grass shore: An inland classic. If you are touring the countryside and see a lake you like the looks of, just find an access way to the shore and take a dip. I do it all the time. Question: How difficult is it to relocate within Europe for a job?
Answer: It depends on the country you are moving to. If you are an EU citizen, it is theoretically very easy to just move to another EU country and set up shop. Having said that, their administrative peculiarities are far from streamlined according to common parameters. I have found it incredibly easy to relocate to the UK when it still belonged to the EU; just arrive, start the job, rent a place, everything just falls into place as if by itself. Healthcare coverage, social system… you basically jump start a chain reaction by starting a job that sets all of these in motion, and any other bits will either come and find you, or advertise their existence in other ways - council tax, TV licence, etc. By contrast, Germany is less easy. You do need to run after quite a few things yourself, and if you fail to chase them down in good time, someone may come down hard on you. France and Austria are also a bit like that. Sweden is perhaps the most demanding obstacle course one can run as an EU citizen though that I have come across. There are a good number of things here you’ve got to have to function normally, but no one tells you what those are, or how you can get them. You’re basically expected to wade into a jungle of Swedish language websites for application processes to things that require each other in unnerving catch 22 style ways, and if you need help, well… you could call a number, from 08:30–09:15, on Thursdays, and hope the English language operator is available… if you even know which number to call, of which administrative body, in which order. It’s mystical, silent, and extremely frustrating. Perhaps similarly challenging is Italy. My cousin tried to establish himself in Italy as a dentist, and was given such a runaround for almost two years that he decided to quit the game and moved to England instead, where he was up and running within 24 hours. Now, having said all that, if you are not an EU citizen and hold some type of residence document from an EU country, it’s an entirely different world again, as you would then need to take up your individual immigration case with the authorities of the country you are moving to. So, no matter how easy it may have been to secure a work permit in country X, and on what criteria, it will be a different story entirely in country Y. Again because immigration policy between the EU countries is in no way aligned, so you may well find yourself back at square one entirely when you try it with another European country.
